lesson.title: Shading Your Way to the Answer: Graphing Systems of Inequalities
lesson.summary: Graphing a system of inequalities means drawing each boundary line, solid or dashed depending on the inequality symbol, and shading the correct half-plane for each, so the overlapping shaded area shows every solution at once.
lesson.body:
Graphing a system of inequalities extends the graphing method used for equations into two new ingredients: the type of boundary line and the direction of shading. For each inequality in the system, first graph its boundary line exactly as you would graph an ordinary line, rewriting it in slope-intercept form if that helps. Use a solid line when the inequality includes equality, less than or equal to or greater than or equal to, since points on the boundary count as solutions, and use a dashed line when the inequality is strict, less than or greater than, since points on the boundary are excluded from the solution set entirely. This solid-versus-dashed distinction has no counterpart when graphing equations, since a single equation's line is always drawn solid.

After drawing each boundary line, shade the half-plane containing that inequality's actual solutions. The most reliable way to decide which side to shade is to pick a convenient test point that is clearly not on the boundary line, often (0, 0) when the line does not pass through the origin, and substitute its coordinates into the inequality. If the resulting statement is true, shade the side of the line containing that test point; if false, shade the opposite side instead, since the true side and the shaded side must always match. This test-point method works for any boundary line and removes any guesswork about which of the two half-planes is the correct one.

Consider the system y <= 2x + 1 and y > -x - 2. Since the first inequality includes equality, its boundary line, y = 2x + 1, is drawn solid. Since the second is strict, its boundary line, y = -x - 2, is drawn dashed. Testing the origin (0, 0) in the first inequality: is 0 less than or equal to 2(0) + 1 = 1? Yes, 0 is less than 1, so shade the side of the solid line that contains the origin. Testing the origin in the second inequality: is 0 greater than -0 - 2 = -2? Yes, 0 is greater than -2, so shade the side of the dashed line that also contains the origin.

Because the origin satisfies both inequalities, it should land inside the overlapping shaded region, and nearby points can confirm this. Check (0, -1): for the first inequality, is -1 less than or equal to 2(0) + 1 = 1? Yes. For the second, is -1 greater than -0 - 2 = -2? Yes, since -1 is greater than -2. Both statements hold, so (0, -1) also lies in the overlap, verifying that the region where the two shadings cover the same area is exactly where solutions of the system live, and any other point chosen from within that overlap would pass both checks the same way.

That overlapping shaded area has a name of its own: the solution region, examined next, and its exact shape depends on how the individual half-planes happen to overlap, whether they form a bounded shape closed in on all sides or an unbounded region that stretches out indefinitely in one or more directions.
